result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of Megalopolis, describing the south-facing part of the city across the river. He lists the theatre, the Thersilium council-chamber, temples, altars and statues, and the large bones said to be a giant's.

scenes.title: Theatre, council-chamber and temples
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the theatre, the Thersilium, Alexander's house and several ruined temples, a racecourse and altars.

scenes.title: The hill sanctuaries and giant's bones
scenes.summary: On the eastern hill are temples of Artemis, Æsculapius and Apollo, and the bones of a giant are kept.

alias_notes.explanation: Apollo as protector of streets, shown as a square pillar.

analysis.text: Pausanias catalogues a city's monuments, showing decay: many temples are ruins in his day.
The Thersilium and the theatre reflect Megalopolis's founding as a federal Arcadian capital in the 4th century BC.

fun_facts.text: The theatre of Megalopolis was among the largest in Greece, and its remains can still be seen.

language_notes.text: Perennial means the spring never dries up, flowing all year round.
Council-chamber translates the Greek bouleuterion, a roofed hall where an assembly met; here it served the Arcadian federal assembly.
Square Hermæ: pillar-shaped statues with a head on a squared shaft, originally images of Hermes. Here the form is used for other gods.
Ammon is the Egyptian god Amun, identified with Zeus and shown with ram's horns; Alexander claimed his divine sonship.
Celestial and Common are the Greek Aphrodite Urania (heavenly love) and Pandemos (of all the people).
Vestibule means the entrance porch of the temple.
Workers: Athene Ergane is Athene as patroness of crafts; Apollo Agyieus is Apollo as guardian of streets and doorways, shown as a pillar.
A cubit is about a foot and a half (roughly 45 cm).
Rhea, mother of Zeus, was aided by giants in Arcadian legend; Pausanias promises the story later.

context_notes.text: Alexander the Great, son of Philip of Macedon, conquered the Persian empire; a house built for him shows the city's Macedonian-era ties.
Dionysus was the god of wine and theatre; lightning was a sign of Zeus's anger or a god's direct action.
Æsculapius was the god of healing; Hygiea, health, was regarded as his daughter.
Ilithyia was the goddess who helped women in childbirth.

literary_notes.text: Only a few foundations remain, a sad contrast with the earlier grandeur; ruin is a recurring theme of this tour of the city.
The promise to narrate the story later links this relic to a larger myth and builds anticipation.
